l: Athenian expedition to Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Athenian expedition to Egypt joined the forces of Inarus and defeated the Persian army in its first battle. It later became trapped on Prosopitis, but the Athenians burned their ships and secured permission to withdraw through Africa and Cyrene.

l: Battle in Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: In the battle in Egypt, the Athenians broke the Persian wing opposing them and caused the Persian army to flee to the White Wall. The victory led to the siege of the remaining Persian forces.

l: Prosopitis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Prosopitis was the island where the Athenian fleet lay at anchor during the Egyptian war. The Persians diverted the river around it, joined it to the mainland, and rendered the fleet useless.

l: Corinthians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Corinthians and Epidaurians began a war against Athens, but the Athenians defeated them. The Corinthians later fought the Megareans over territorial boundaries and were defeated by the Athenians assisting Megara.

l: Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Athenians invaded Peloponnesus after defeating their opponents in battle and killed and destroyed many of their enemies there.

l: Leocrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Leocrates commanded the Athenian fleet during the nine-month war against the Aeginetans. Under his leadership, the Athenians defeated the Aeginetans and captured or destroyed seventy of their vessels.

l: Megareans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Megareans, fearing their weakness against Corinth, formed a league with Athens. With Athenian assistance under Myronides, they resisted the Corinthian army.

l: Megara, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Megara became allied with Athens during its conflict with Corinth. Athenian forces sent to Megara defeated the Corinthian army in successive battles.

l: war between Corinth and Megara, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The war between Corinth and Megara began over the boundaries of their territories. After raids and minor skirmishes, Megara allied with Athens, which defeated the Corinthian forces.

l: Myronides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Myronides commanded the Athenian forces sent to assist Megara against Corinth. His army defeated the Corinthians in a hard-fought battle and won another victory at Cimolia.

l: Phocians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Phocians made war against the Dorians and initially defeated them, taking their cities. They were later defeated by the Lacedaemonians under Nicomedes, who recovered the Dorian cities.

l: Dorians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Dorians inhabited Cytinium, Boium, and Erineus beneath Mount Parnassus. After losing their cities to the Phocians, they received Lacedaemonian aid and recovered them.

l: Phocian war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Phocian war began with a Phocian attack on the Dorian cities. Nicomedes led Lacedaemonian and Peloponnesian forces to defeat the Phocians and end the conflict through a peace agreement.

l: Argives, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Argives joined the Athenians against the Lacedaemonians and Thessalians. They fought alongside the Athenians at Tanagra.

l: Thessalians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Thessalians initially assisted the Athenians but deserted during the Battle of Tanagra and joined the Spartans. They later attacked Athenian provisions at night before being routed by the Athenians.

l: Tanagra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Tanagra in Boeotia was the place toward which the Lacedaemonians turned while returning from the Phocian war. The Athenians followed them there, and the opposing armies fought.

l: Battle of Tanagra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Battle of Tanagra was fought between the Athenians and their allies and the Lacedaemonians and their allies. The Thessalians changed sides, many were killed, and the battle ended without a decisive result when night fell.

l: Deucetius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Deucetius, general and later king of the Sicilians, built Menenum and divided its neighboring lands by lot. He also made war against Catana over land claimed by the Sicilians.

l: Catana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Catana's inhabitants defended lands assigned to them when Hiero established the colony. After being defeated by Deucetius and the Syracusans, they left Catana for Etna, while the former inhabitants returned.

l: Mount Etna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Etna, formerly called Eunetia, became the refuge of the Cataneans after they were forced to leave Catana.

l: Sicilian restoration of the old commonwealths, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Sicilian cities eventually expelled foreign usurpers, restored those who had been banished, and returned to their ancient forms of commonwealth. Public lands were divided by lot among the citizens, while foreigners were transplanted to Messana.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: The Thebans, supported by the Lacedaemonians, sought to recover control of Boeotia, but Myronides led the Athenians to victory over them and then campaigned through Boeotia, Locris, Phocis, and Thessaly. Tolmides later invaded Laconia and attacked Spartan possessions, while Pericles conducted further Athenian campaigns in Peloponnesus and Acarnania. In Sicily, the Syracusans adopted Petalism, an olive-leaf form of ostracism, but soon abolished it after it encouraged disorder and drove useful citizens from public life. Deucetius united the Siculi, founded Palicon near the temple of the Palici, and the text describes the temple’s extraordinary Craters and sacred functions.

l: Thebans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: The Thebans, weakened because of their league with Xerxes, sought Lacedaemonian assistance in recovering authority over Boeotia. They were defeated by Myronides and subsequently lost control of most of Boeotia, although Thebes remained unconquered.

l: Boeotians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Many Boeotians had shaken off Theban authority, prompting the Thebans to seek Lacedaemonian support. The Boeotians later assembled a large army against the Athenians, but were defeated after a day-long battle among their vineyards.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: The Lacedaemonians supported the Thebans because they viewed Thebes as a useful bulwark against Athens. They enlarged Thebes and compelled the Boeotians to submit to Theban rule, later sending aid to Sicyon when Pericles besieged it.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: The Athenians raised armies under Myronides, Tolmides, and Pericles and won several victories and cities. They defeated the Thebans, campaigned through Boeotia and neighboring regions, invaded Peloponnesus, and made a five-year peace with the Peloponnesians.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Athens appointed Mnesitheides, Callias, Ariston, and Lysicrates as archons in the successive years described. Its people authorized Tolmides’s expedition and welcomed Myronides after his successful campaigns.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Thebes was enlarged by the Lacedaemonians and made the center of control over Boeotia. Myronides captured most Boeotian cities but did not capture Thebes.

l: Boeotia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Boeotia was brought under Theban authority with Lacedaemonian assistance. Myronides defeated the Boeotians, stormed and demolished Tanagra, ravaged the country, and soon won all its cities except Thebes.

l: Myronides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Myronides led the Athenians against the Thebans despite having fewer soldiers than expected, arguing that those who appeared on the appointed day showed greater courage. He defeated the Thebans, captured and demolished Tanagra, ravaged Boeotia, overcame the Locrians and Phocians, besieged Pharsalus unsuccessfully, and returned to Athens with great acclaim.

l: Battle between the Athenians and the Thebans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: The battle ended in a decisive Athenian victory under Myronides. The text gives no detailed account of its order or manner, but considers it at least equal to Athens’s greatest earlier victories because the Athenians defeated the reputedly bravest Greeks without relying on confederates.

l: Tanagra campaign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Myronides marched into Boeotia, defeated the enemy, and immediately took Tanagra by storm. He demolished the city and distributed the country’s spoil and riches among his soldiers.

l: Tolmides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Tolmides, an Athenian admiral, persuaded Athens to authorize an invasion of Laconia and secretly recruited more than the proposed thousand men. He sailed with fifty ships and four thousand soldiers, took Methone and Gytheum, destroyed Spartan shipping and naval stores, subdued Cephalenia, captured Naupactus, and later continued operations in Boeotia and Euboea.

l: Spartans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: The Spartans were targeted by Tolmides, who invaded their territory and attacked their ports. They quickly sent aid to Methone, forcing Tolmides to withdraw from it.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Sparta’s glory was challenged by Tolmides, who promised to bring an eclipse upon it through an invasion of Laconia. The text does not report that Tolmides captured Sparta.

l: Laconia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Laconia was invaded by Tolmides with an Athenian fleet and army. He took Methone and Gytheum, destroyed ships and naval provisions, and ravaged the surrounding country.

l: Pericles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Pericles led Athenian expeditions into Peloponnesus, Acarnania, Chersonesus, and against the Naxians. He defeated the Sicyonians, besieged Sicyon until Lacedaemonian aid arrived, ravaged the country of the Oeniadae, and divided conquered lands among Athenian citizens.

l: Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Peloponnesus was invaded and ravaged by Pericles, who attacked Sicyon and the country of the Oeniadae. A five-year peace was later made between the Athenians and the Peloponnesians.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Sicily was affected by war between the Aegesteans and Lilybaeans and by civil disorder at Syracuse. The Syracusans introduced Petalism after repeated attempts by ambitious men to seize power, but later repealed it.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: The Syracusans executed Tyndarides and other innovators after rescuers freed him from custody. They adopted Petalism to prevent powerful citizens from pursuing sovereignty, later sent fleets against the Tyrrhenians, and eventually abolished Petalism because it encouraged disorder and drove valuable citizens from public life.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Syracuse suffered from civil dissension connected with land allotments and attempts to establish tyranny. Its citizens created and later repealed Petalism after factional leaders and disorder became more influential.

l: ostracism, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Ostracism at Athens is described as the model for the Syracusan practice of Petalism. It involved voting to banish a citizen considered powerful enough to seek sovereignty, rather than punishing a specific crime.

l: Petalism, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Petalism was Syracuse’s version of ostracism, in which citizens wrote the name of a potentially dominant man on an olive leaf and banished the person receiving the most votes for five years. It was repealed after leading citizens withdrew from public affairs and disorder increased.

l: olive-leaf voting, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Olive-leaf voting required Syracusans to write on an olive leaf the name of the citizen they thought most capable of seizing power. The person whose name appeared on the greatest number of leaves was banished for five years.

l: Deucetius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Deucetius, prince of the Siculi, united nearly all the Siculi cities into one community. He moved Neas to a plain, founded Palicon near the temple of the Palici, and distributed the surrounding country among the inhabitants.

l: Palicon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: Palicon was founded by Deucetius near the temple of the Palici and became prosperous because of its fertile land and numerous inhabitants. The city was later destroyed and left waste and deserted.

l: temple of the Palici, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: The temple of the Palici was regarded as exceptionally ancient and sacred, and it was associated with solemn oaths, punishment of perjurers, and refuge for abused servants. It stood in a pleasant plain with porches, galleries, and other buildings, and was located near Palicon.

l: Craters, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXIV.
s: The Craters were deep hollows in the ground at the temple of the Palici from which fire and water were said to burst upward with sulfurous fumes and terrifying noise. They were treated as a divine wonder, and the sacred site was used for oaths whose violation was believed to bring punishment.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXVIII.
s: Deucetius, general of the Siculi, captured Aetna and then invaded the country of the Agrigentines, taking Motya after defeating forces sent to relieve it. The Syracusans later defeated Deucetius in battle, while the Agrigentines retook Motya and joined the Syracusans. Deucetius fled to Syracuse and submitted himself and his country as a suppliant. The Syracusans spared him and sent him to Corinth, promising to provide for his needs.

l: Deucetius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXVIII.
s: Deucetius, the general of the Siculi, took Aetna and invaded the country of the Agrigentines, capturing Motya after defeating an Agrigentine relief force. He was later defeated by the Syracusans, abandoned by many of his soldiers, and deprived of his treasure. He fled to Syracuse, submitted as a suppliant, and was sent to Corinth with a promise of support.

l: Siculi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXVIII.
s: The Siculi followed Deucetius in his campaign against the Agrigentines. They fought bravely near Nomae but were eventually routed, and many were killed during the pursuit; others fled to forts and strongholds.

l: Agrigentines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXVIII.
s: The Agrigentines sent aid to Motya, but Deucetius defeated them and captured the place. They later retook Motya by force and joined the victorious Syracusans in encampment.

l: Motya, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXVIII.
s: Motya was an Agrigentine garrison that Deucetius besieged and captured after defeating an Agrigentine relief force. The Agrigentines later retook its castle, which contained a garrison belonging to Deucetius.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXVIII.
s: The Syracusans killed Bilco, their general, believing him responsible for their defeat and suspecting him of secret communication with Deucetius. They later defeated Deucetius, accepted his submission as a suppliant, and sent him to Corinth with a promise to supply his necessities.

l: battle between Deucetius and the Agrigentines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXVIII.
s: Deucetius fought the Agrigentines when they sent aid to Motya. His army defeated them and captured the place.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXVIII.
s: Syracuse was the place to which Deucetius fled at night and where he sought protection by falling before the altars in the market-place. Its assembly decided to preserve him as a suppliant rather than punish him.

l: Corinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXVIII.
s: Corinth was the place to which the Syracusans sent Deucetius after accepting his submission. They commanded him to remain there for the rest of his life and promised to provide what was necessary for his comfortable support.

l: submission of Deucetius to the Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XXVIII.
s: After his defeat and the desertion of many of his soldiers, Deucetius went to Syracuse and submitted himself and his country as a suppliant. The Syracusans unanimously resolved to spare him and sent him to Corinth.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: The unit recounts how Xerxes’ invasion of Greece threatened Greek freedom but ultimately brought Greece wealth, renown, and cultural flourishing. Cimon led an Athenian expedition against Cyprus, defeated Persian forces, and helped secure the Peace of Callias, under which the Greek cities in Asia were freed. After Cimon died in Cyprus, the Megareans revolted from Athens, and the Athenians later suffered defeat at Chaeronea, forcing them to restore Boeotian cities to their ancient liberties. Further revolts and Pericles’ campaign in Euboea led to a thirty-year peace.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Xerxes led an expedition into Greece with a vast army, terrifying the Greeks and threatening to reduce them to slavery. His invasion ultimately failed, and Greece gained enduring renown and prosperity.

l: Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Persia threatened Greece through Xerxes’ invasion and had previously brought the Greek cities in Asia under its power. Persian forces were later defeated by the Athenians, and Persia agreed to terms freeing the Greek cities in Asia.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Greece was threatened with enslavement by Xerxes’ invasion but was unexpectedly delivered from the danger. It then flourished for fifty years, becoming wealthy and advancing in arts, sciences, philosophy, and oratory.

l: the Greek cities of Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: The Greek cities in Asia had been brought under Persian power before Xerxes’ invasion. Under the peace between Persia and the Athenians, they were to be free and governed by their own laws.

l: Cimon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Cimon, the son of Miltiades, commanded the Athenian expedition against Cyprus. He captured Citium and Malus, defeated Persian forces by sea and land, helped secure peace with Persia, and died of illness in Cyprus.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: The Athenians sent forces against Persia to secure the liberty of the Greek cities in Asia. They accepted peace with Persia, withdrew from Cyprus after their victories, and later fought against the Megareans and other revolting communities.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Athens became highly honored after its victories over Persia and was especially distinguished for philosophy and oratory. It made peace with Persia, fought the Megareans, suffered defeat at Chaeronea, and later concluded a thirty-year peace.

l: Cyprian war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: The Cyprian war began with the Athenian expedition against Persian power in Cyprus. It ended when peace was made between Persia and the Athenians, after which the Athenians withdrew their forces.

l: Cyprus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Cyprus was invaded by Cimon and the Athenians, who captured several cities and brought most of the island under Athenian power. Salamis remained under a strong Persian garrison until peace ended the campaign, and Cimon died on the island.

l: Athenian expedition against Cyprus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: The Athenians sent two hundred galleys under Cimon to invade Persian-held Cyprus. The expedition captured Citium and Malus, defeated Persian naval and land forces, and withdrew after peace was concluded.

l: Athenian navy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: The Athenians equipped a navy of two hundred galleys for the campaign against Cyprus. Under Cimon, it defeated the Persian fleet, sank many vessels, captured one hundred ships, and controlled the sea around Cyprus.

l: Artabazus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Artabazus commanded the Persian fleet, which numbered three hundred ships and was stationed at Cyprus. After the Persian defeats, he and Megabyzus sent ambassadors to Athens to negotiate peace.

l: Megabyzus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Megabyzus commanded the Persian land forces and had an army of three hundred thousand men encamped in Cilicia. After the Persian defeats, he joined Artabazus in sending ambassadors to Athens to negotiate peace.

l: Salamis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Salamis was the metropolis of Cyprus and contained a strong Persian garrison with abundant arms, ammunition, and provisions. Cimon considered its capture essential to securing the whole island, but the garrison successfully defended the city during the siege.

l: Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Artaxerxes, king of Persia, convened a council after hearing that Persian armies had been defeated in Cyprus. The council decided that Persia should make peace with the Greeks, and Artaxerxes’ officers were ordered to negotiate on any terms.

l: Peace of Callias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: The peace required Persia to free the Greek cities in Asia and keep its commanders and warships away from specified areas near the Greek coast. The Athenians agreed not to invade any province of Artaxerxes, and the peace led them to withdraw from Cyprus.

l: Megareans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: The Megareans revolted from the Athenians and made a league with Sparta through their ambassadors. The Athenians invaded their country, plundered it, and defeated the Megareans when they came out to defend it.

l: Tolmides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Tolmides, the Athenian general, captured Chaeronea. The Boeotians then surprised his forces, and Tolmides was killed while fighting bravely.

l: Boeotia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Boeotian forces joined together and defeated Tolmides at Chaeronea. Their victory compelled the Athenians to restore all the cities of Boeotia under their control to their ancient liberties.

l: Battle of Chaeronea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: The Battle of Chaeronea followed Tolmides’ capture of the city. The Boeotians defeated the Athenians, killing or capturing the Athenian forces and forcing Athens to restore the Boeotian cities to their ancient liberties.

l: Chaeronea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIL
s: Chaeronea was captured by Tolmides, the Athenian general. The Boeotians then surprised the Athenian forces there and won a bloody battle.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ne H*ar between the AgngetUines and Sgracu»ans in Sicily. Uie
s: A war arose in Sicily between the Syracusans and the Agrigentines after the Syracusans pardoned Deucetius and sent him to lead a private life at Corinth without consulting the Agrigentines. Deucetius later returned to Sicily to establish a colony, and some Siculi joined him. The Siculi divided between the two sides, and the Syracusans and Agrigentines raised large armies. The Syracusans defeated the Agrigentines at the river Himera, killing a thousand of them, after which the Agrigentines sent ambassadors to Syracuse to seek peace.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ne H*ar between the AgngetUines and Sgracu»ans in Sicily. Uie
s: The Syracusans broke the power of Deucetius, pardoned him upon his submission to the people, and commanded him to lead a private life at Corinth. They later fought the Agrigentines at the river Himera and won the battle, killing a thousand Agrigentines.

l: Agrigentines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ne H*ar between the AgngetUines and Sgracu»ans in Sicily. Uie
s: The Agrigentines became angry with the Syracusans because they had spared Deucetius without their consent and because of envy of the Syracusans. They made war upon the Syracusans, were defeated at the river Himera, and afterward sent ambassadors to Syracuse to make peace.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ne H*ar between the AgngetUines and Sgracu»ans in Sicily. Uie
s: Syracuse was the city whose people pardoned Deucetius and sent him to Corinth. After the battle at the river Himera, it received Agrigentine ambassadors seeking peace.

l: Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ne H*ar between the AgngetUines and Sgracu»ans in Sicily. Uie
s: Agrigentum was the city associated with the Agrigentines, who made war upon the Syracusans after Deucetius was spared without their consent.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ne H*ar between the AgngetUines and Sgracu»ans in Sicily. Uie
s: Sicily was the setting of the war between the Agrigentines and Syracusans. Deucetius returned there with many men to establish a colony, and cities of the Siculi divided between the two sides.

l: war between the Agrigentines and Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ne H*ar between the AgngetUines and Sgracu»ans in Sicily. Uie
s: The war arose in Sicily after the Syracusans pardoned Deucetius and sent him to Corinth without consulting the Agrigentines. The Siculi divided between the two sides, large armies were raised, and the Syracusans defeated the Agrigentines at the river Himera; the Agrigentines then sought peace.

l: Deucetius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ne H*ar between the AgngetUines and Sgracu»ans in Sicily. Uie
s: Deucetius was the prince of the Siculi whose power the Syracusans broke. After submitting to the people, he was pardoned and commanded to live privately at Corinth, but he later broke his agreements, returned to Sicily, and brought many men to establish a colony; some Siculi, including Archonides, prince of Erbita, joined him.

l: battle at the river Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ne H*ar between the AgngetUines and Sgracu»ans in Sicily. Uie
s: The Syracusans and Agrigentines met in battle at the river Himera after camping opposite each other. The Syracusans won and killed a thousand Agrigentines on the field.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: The unit recounts the destruction of Sybaris by the Crotonians and the subsequent founding of Thurium by Sybarite exiles, Athenians, and other Greek colonists. Thurium was initially troubled by conflict between the ancient Sybarite inhabitants and the new colonists, but the new colonists eventually gained control and established a democracy. Charondas was chosen as legislator and created laws concerning family life, false accusation, harmful associations, education, orphans, military service, and the amendment of laws. The unit also describes several successful challenges to Charondas’s laws and his remarkable death by deliberately enforcing his own prohibition against entering the assembly armed.

l: Thurium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: Thurium was built in Italy near a spring called Thuria, which the colonists believed fulfilled an oracle promising a city with little water and abundant bread. Its streets were laid out in a compact and beautiful plan, but conflict soon arose between the ancient Sybarite inhabitants and the new colonists. After the new colonists destroyed almost all the ancient inhabitants, Thurium became wealthy, allied with the Crotonians, and was governed as a democracy.

l: Sybaris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: Sybaris became wealthy and populous because of its fertile territory between the Crathis and Sybaris rivers, and it was said to have three hundred thousand inhabitants. Under the influence of Telys, it banished five hundred wealthy citizens and confiscated their estates. After the Crotonians defeated its army, the city was sacked and laid waste; although it was rebuilt by the Thessalians, they were later expelled by the Crotonians.

l: Crotona, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: Crotona received the Sybarite exiles who sought refuge at its altars. Although its people initially hesitated to protect them against Sybaris, they decided to fight after Pythagoras advised them to defend the suppliants. Crotona defeated Sybaris and later expelled the Thessalians who had rebuilt the city.

l: Thurium’s founding colony, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: The founding colony of Thurium consisted of Sybarite exiles assisted by Athenians and other Greeks. The Athenians sent ten ships under Lampo and Xenocrates, while heralds invited people from the cities of Peloponnesus to join the colony. The colonists settled near the spring called Thuria and named their city Thurium.

l: Telys, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: Telys had great influence over the people of Sybaris and stirred up scandals against the wealthiest citizens. He persuaded the Sybarites to banish five hundred wealthy men and confiscate their estates, and he then demanded that Crotona surrender the exiles or face war.

l: Sybarites, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: The Sybarites banished their wealthiest citizens and went to war against Crotona when Crotona protected the exiles. Their army was defeated, and most of it was destroyed while Sybaris was sacked. The surviving Sybarites later sought aid from the Lacedaemonians and Athenians to recover their country and establish a new colony.

l: the Crotonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: The Crotonians protected the Sybarite suppliants after initially considering surrendering them. Under Milo’s command, they defeated the much larger Sybarite army, gave no quarter, and destroyed Sybaris. They later expelled the Thessalians who had rebuilt the city and formed an alliance with the inhabitants of Thurium.

l: the new Greek colonists, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: The new Greek colonists at Thurium were initially disadvantaged by the ancient Sybarites, who reserved the chief magistracies, the first sacrificial honors for their wives, and the land nearest the city for themselves. Because the new colonists were more powerful, they eventually destroyed almost all the ancient inhabitants and took control of the city. They then invited additional people from Greece to cultivate and improve the rich country.

l: the Thurian citizens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: The Thurian citizens became wealthy after inviting people from Greece to settle and cultivate the land. They divided themselves into ten tribes named according to their regions of origin and chose Charondas as their legislator. Their laws addressed family conduct, false accusation, harmful company, education, guardianship, military service, and the preservation of legal authority.

l: the Thurian democracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: The Thurian democracy was established after the new colonists gained control of the city. Under it, the citizens were divided into ten tribes, and Charondas was appointed to organize their laws. The people also voted on proposed alterations to the laws, with the proposer risking execution if the change was rejected.

l: Charondas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: Charondas was chosen as Thurium’s legislator because he was regarded as learned and accomplished. He examined the laws of different countries, selected what he considered best, and added laws of his own concerning marriage, false accusations, harmful associations, education, orphans, military duty, and legal amendments. He died by deliberately running himself through with his sword after entering an assembly armed, contrary to a law he had made.

l: good laws of Charondas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: Charondas’s laws excluded from public office men who brought a second wife and stepmother into their households, punished false accusers by parading them through the city crowned with tamarisk, and fined those who kept company with wicked men. They also regulated orphan guardianship, punished cowardice with public humiliation rather than death, and required strict obedience to the wording of the law. One law required anyone proposing a legal alteration to wear a rope around his neck until the people voted, with rejection resulting in hanging; several later proposals nevertheless succeeded in amending particular laws.

l: public education in writing, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, agreed on upon certain conditions. Whilst things were thus acting
s: Charondas required all citizens’ children to learn writing, with the city paying the teachers’ wages. He considered writing especially important because it preserved votes, decrees, letters, wills, laws, knowledge, and the memory of the dead for future generations. The measure gave poor children access to instruction that their families could not otherwise afford.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But having spoken enough of Charondas, we shall now relate
s: The unit concerns Zaleuchus, an Italian law-maker born at Locris, who was a scholar of Pythagoras and was chosen by his people to make their laws. His laws began by requiring belief in the gods, worship of them, and purity of mind and conduct. They also instructed people to reconcile with adversaries, directed magistrates not to be proud or partial, and restricted the public behavior and luxury of women and certain men through dishonorable exceptions.

l: Zaleuchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But having spoken enough of Charondas, we shall now relate
s: Zaleuchus was an Italian born at Locris, of noble family, greatly learned, and a scholar of Pythagoras. He was highly esteemed in his country and was chosen by the people to be their law-maker.

l: Locris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But having spoken enough of Charondas, we shall now relate
s: Locris was the place where Zaleuchus was born. Its people chose him to make their laws.

l: the inhabitants of Locris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But having spoken enough of Charondas, we shall now relate
s: The inhabitants were required by Zaleuchus's laws to believe fully in the gods, worship them, and keep their minds pure. They were also instructed not to remain implacable toward one another but to preserve the possibility of reconciliation and friendship with their adversaries.

l: the gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But having spoken enough of Charondas, we shall now relate
s: The gods were presented in Zaleuchus's preface as the source from whom all good descends upon men. They were said to be more pleased by the just and honest actions of righteous people than by costly sacrifices.

l: laws of Zaleucus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But having spoken enough of Charondas, we shall now relate
s: The laws of Zaleuchus began with the worship of the gods and included rules on reconciliation, the conduct of magistrates, and the behavior and adornment of women and men. They restricted women's attendants, nighttime walks, and luxurious ornaments through dishonorable exceptions.

l: magistrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But having spoken enough of Charondas, we shall now relate
s: The magistrates were commanded not to be proud or domineering. They were also forbidden to give judgment in any matter for love or hatred.

l: women, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But having spoken enough of Charondas, we shall now relate
s: Free women of the city were forbidden to be attended abroad by more than one servant unless they were drunk. They were also forbidden to walk abroad at night or wear golden ornaments or garments embroidered with gold unless they intended to play the whore.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The Decemviri's abuse of power in Rome led to the young woman's death and provoked the soldiers at Algidum to seize the Aventine mount. The crisis was settled by creating ten tribunes of the people with broad authority, requiring that one consul come from the senators and the other from the common people, and allowing both consuls to be chosen from the common people if desired. Marcus Horatius and Lucius Valerius Potitus were then made consuls and completed the Roman laws by adding the final two of the twelve tables. The period ended with peace in Rome and throughout much of the known world.

l: Marcus Claudius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: Marcus Claudius was identified as the fellow who claimed the young woman as his bondslave and obtained judgment against her before the Decemviri. He carried her away as a bondmaid after the corrupt judgment.

l: Marcus Huratius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: Marcus Horatius was created consul with Lucius Valerius Potitus. He helped complete the Roman laws by adding the final two tables.

l: Lucius Valerius Potitus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: Lucius Valerius Potitus was created consul with Marcus Horatius. He helped complete the Roman laws by adding the final two tables.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: Rome was the scene of the conflict between the Decemviri and the soldiers who opposed the abuse of power. The soldiers entered Rome and seized the Aventine mount, after which the dispute was settled by political concessions and the city returned to order.

l: Algidum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: Algidum was the place where the army was encamped when the young woman's father came to report his calamity and seek assistance.

l: Aventine mount, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The soldiers entered Rome at night and took possession of the Aventine mount during their revolt against the Decemviri's conduct.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The Romans created Marcus Horatius and Lucius Valerius Potitus as consuls. They subsequently had the completed laws engraved on twelve brass tables and placed before the court.

l: the patricians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The patricians were said to have used their high birth and family glory to arrogate all the power and authority of Rome to themselves. The new arrangements were made as a check on their excessive power.

l: the common people, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The common people were granted representation through ten tribunes of the people. The settlement also provided that one consul should be chosen from the common people, and that both consuls could be chosen from them if considered appropriate.

l: the Decemviri, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The Decemviri were responsible for judging the young woman's case, and one of them used his authority to obtain her as a bondslave through a corrupt judgment. When the soldiers revolted, the Decemviri gathered young men and prepared to defend their colleague by force.

l: Roman tribunes of the people, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The settlement required ten tribunes of the people to be chosen with sovereign authority over the other magistrates and power to protect the people's liberty. They were to appoint successors at the end of each year, under penalty of being burned alive if they neglected this duty; if they could not agree on a choice, they were to remain in office meanwhile.

l: Roman consuls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The consuls were required by the settlement to include one person chosen from the senators and one from the common people, with both permitted to come from the common people if desired. Marcus Horatius and Lucius Valerius Potitus later served as consuls and completed the laws.

l: the twelve tables, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: Ten of the twelve tables had already been completed when Marcus Horatius and Lucius Valerius Potitus became consuls. The two consuls added the remaining two, and the complete set was engraved on twelve brass tables.

l: the Roman laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The Roman laws were completed after the sedition, when the final two tables were added. They were engraved briefly and plainly on twelve brass tables and fixed before the court.

l: the laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The laws were made to check the excessive power of the patricians and to establish protections for the common people. After being completed, they were publicly engraved on brass tables in front of the court.

l: the great commotion at Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The great commotion at Rome ended when the parties agreed to establish ten tribunes of the people and alter the selection of consuls. The settlement brought the conflict to a close.

l: the sedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The sedition disrupted the laws being prepared by the Decemviri. After it, Marcus Horatius and Lucius Valerius Potitus completed the law code by adding two tables.

l: the soldiers' revolt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The soldiers' revolt began after the young woman's father reported her mistreatment and death to the army at Algidum. The soldiers entered Rome, seized the Aventine mount, and forced a settlement that expanded popular authority.

l: the young woman, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The young woman was a beautiful virgin of small fortune whom Marcus Claudius desired and tried to debauch. After a corrupt judgment declared her a bondslave, her father stabbed her to death to spare her the indignity and disgrace of that condition.

l: the young woman's father, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The young woman's father followed her after she had been carried away as a bondmaid. He stabbed her with a knife from a butcher's shop, fled Rome, and went to the army at Algidum to ask for assistance.

l: the army at Algidum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, great and high birth, and the glory of their families, with inaaflierabk
s: The army at Algidum heard the young woman's father's account of his calamity and was moved by pity and sorrow. Its soldiers then entered Rome at night and took possession of the Aventine mount.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Samians went to war with the Milesians over Priene and revolted from Athens, but Pericles captured Samos, imposed a fine, and took hostages. A later sedition in Samos enabled the aristocratic faction, aided by Pisuthnes and Persian soldiers, to seize the city and renew the war; after naval battles and a prolonged siege, Pericles retook Samos, punished the revolt's leaders, and restored democracy. In Sicily, the Syracusans attacked Trinacria, defeated and destroyed the city, enslaved its inhabitants, and sent the richest spoils to Delphi.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Athens favored the Milesians in their dispute with the Samians. It sent Pericles against Samos and later supplied him with additional ships.

l: Samians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Samians fought the Milesians over Priene and revolted from Athens. After Pericles initially subdued them, factions in Samos restored their independence with Persian aid; they defeated part of Pericles' fleet, but were eventually defeated, fined, disarmed, and subjected to a restored democracy.

l: Milesians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Milesians were involved in a war with the Samians concerning Priene. The Athenians favored them in that conflict.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Athenians sent Pericles with forty ships against the Samians, later reinforced him with sixty ships, and also received thirty ships from Chios and Mitylene for the renewed siege.

l: Pericles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Pericles captured Samos, established a democracy there, imposed a fine of eighty talents, and took youths as hostages. After the Samians revolted again, he defeated them at sea, besieged Samos, confronted the Phoenician fleet, recovered from the defeat of his detached ships, and finally captured the city, punished the revolt's leaders, restored democracy, and returned to Athens.

l: Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Samos was first reduced by Pericles and placed under a democracy. During a later sedition, the opposing faction seized the city with Persian assistance, but Pericles eventually captured it after a siege, demolished its walls, removed its ships, and restored its democracy.

l: Samian revolt from Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Samians revolted from Athens because they perceived that Athens favored the Milesians in the dispute over Priene. Pericles suppressed the revolt, imposed an eighty-talent fine, and took hostages.

l: Athenian-Samian war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Athenian-Samian war began with the Samian revolt and resumed after an aristocratic faction, aided by Persian soldiers, seized Samos. It ended when Pericles captured Samos, executed the revolt's leaders, imposed a payment of two hundred talents, took the ships, demolished the walls, and restored democracy.

l: sedition in Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: A sedition divided Samos between supporters of democracy and supporters of an aristocracy. The anti-democratic faction obtained seven hundred soldiers from Pisuthnes, seized the city, expelled the opposing faction, and took back the hostages from Lemnos.

l: naval battle between Athens and Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Pericles defeated the Samians in a sea fight even though they had seventy ships and he had sixty. Later, when Pericles departed with part of his forces, the Samians attacked and routed the portion of his fleet left behind.

l: Phoenician fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Phoenician fleet was sent by the Persians to aid the Samians. Pericles left part of his forces besieging Samos and went to confront it, allowing the Samians to attack and rout the rest of his fleet.

l: siege of Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Pericles besieged Samos by sea and land after defeating the Samians in a naval battle. He used battering rams and scorpions, with the assistance of Artemon the Lacedaemonian, and continued assaults until the walls were breached.

l: fall of Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Samos fell to Pericles after his engines battered down its walls. He executed the authors of the defection, required the Samians to pay two hundred talents, removed their ships, demolished their walls, and restored democracy.

l: Siculi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Siculi were the people over whom Deucetius sought sovereign power after settling colonies in the country of the Callatines. The Syracusans controlled all their cities except Trinacria, whose inhabitants were related to them as kindred.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Syracusans controlled the Sicilian cities except Trinacria and attacked Trinacria because of jealousy of its wealth and fear that it might gain sovereignty over the Siculi. They defeated the Trinacrians, enslaved the inhabitants, destroyed the city, and sent the richest spoils to Delphi.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Syracuse was the power directing the attack against Trinacria. Its forces and confederates defeated the Trinacrians and destroyed their city.

l: Trinacria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Trinacria was the only Sicilian city not under Syracusan control. It was wealthy and known for its many valiant men and commanders, but after receiving no assistance it was defeated, its inhabitants were enslaved, and the city was razed.

l: Syracusan war against Trinacria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Syracusans gathered forces from Syracuse and their confederates to conquer Trinacria. The war ended with the defeat and destruction of Trinacria and the enslavement of its inhabitants.

l: battle between Syracuse and Trinacria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: In a bloody battle, the Trinacrians made a resolute resistance but were hard pressed and all died on the spot. The wounded killed themselves rather than become captives, and the Syracusans won the victory.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Corinthian war began when Epidamnus, a colony associated with Corcyra and Corinth, was troubled by civil strife and appealed for aid, leading Corinth and Corcyra into conflict. Corinth and Corcyra prepared fleets, fought at sea, and drew Athens into an alliance with Corcyra, whose intervention helped secure victory over Corinth. Corinth and Macedonia then encouraged revolts at Potidea and among the cities of Chalcidica, prompting Athens to besiege Potidea and defeat a relieving force near Pallene. During the same period, the Romans fought the Volsci, colonies were established in Italy, and Thucydides began his history of the war between Athens and the Lacedaemonians.

l: Corinthian war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Corinthian war arose from the conflict over Epidamnus between Corinth and Corcyra. Corinth and Corcyra later prepared larger fleets, while Athens joined Corcyra and the conflict contributed to the revolt of Potidea.

l: Epidamnus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Epidamnus suffered civil disturbances in which the stronger faction expelled many members of the opposing faction. The exiles allied with the Illyrians, seized the surrounding country, and besieged the city, leading the inhabitants to seek aid first from Corcyra and then from Corinth.

l: Corcyra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Corcyra refused initial aid to Epidamnus, but later sent a fleet against the Corinthian-supported settlement. Its fleet defeated Corinth, recovered Epidamnus by storm, and later became dominant in that part of the sea before seeking assistance from Athens.

l: Corinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Corinth aided Epidamnus by sending citizens and soldiers, partly from pity and partly because of an old grievance against Corcyra. After losing a naval battle, Corinth rebuilt its fleet, secured ships from its confederates, and later sent forces to support Potidea.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Athens allied itself with Corcyra and sent ships that helped the Corcyreans defeat Corinth at sea. Athens also sent a colony to Amphipolis, supported the revolt-related conflict at Potidea, and besieged that city.

l: Corinthian war at sea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Corinth and Corcyra built and assembled fleets for renewed fighting after Corinth's first defeat. In the later battle, Corinth had 150 ships and Corcyra 120, but Athenian ships arrived and helped Corcyra win; Corinth then avoided another engagement in harbor.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Romans fought the Volsci and won a formal battle, killing many of their opponents. They also appointed consuls or military tribunes in successive years, sent new colonies to Ardea, and killed Spurius Manius after he sought sovereignty.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: In Italy, the Campanians began to flourish because of the fertility of their country. The Tarentines expelled the inhabitants of Siris, brought a new colony there, and built Heraclea.

l: Athenian alliance with Corcyra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: After hearing appeals from both Corcyra and Corinth, Athens decided to join Corcyra. Athens first sent ten ships and later sent twenty more, whose arrival helped the Corcyreans win the naval battle.

l: Potidea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Potidea revolted from Athens after the Corinthians stirred up the city, while Perdiccas persuaded other cities of Chalcidica to revolt. Athens sent forces against Potidea and laid siege to it after defeating the opposing forces near Pallene.

l: Potidean revolt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Potidean revolt was encouraged by Corinth and by Perdiccas, who was hostile to Athens. Athens responded by sending a fleet and army to destroy the rebels' country and storm the city.

l: Battle near Pallene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: A great battle was fought in the isthmus near Pallene between the Athenians and forces supporting Potidea. The Athenians won and killed more than three hundred of the enemy.

l: Athenian siege of Potidea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: After the Athenian victory near Pallene, the siege of Potidea was formally established. Callias died in a later Athenian victory at Potidea, and Phormio succeeded him and continued the siege with repeated assaults.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The text identifies the war between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians as the Peloponnesian war. It states that the war lasted twenty-seven years, while Thucydides wrote only about its first twenty-two years.

l: Phormio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Phormio succeeded Callias as Athenian general after Callias was killed at Potidea. He renewed the siege and pressed the defenders with continual assaults, but the city's resistance prolonged the siege.

l: Thucydides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Thucydides begins his history in this unit and proceeds to relate the war between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians, called the Peloponnesian war. The text says that he wrote about the first twenty-two years of the twenty-seven-year conflict.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: The unit describes the causes and opening campaigns of the Peloponnesian war between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians. Pericles urged Athens to resist the Lacedaemonians, relying on Athenian wealth, allies, and naval strength, while the Lacedaemonians invaded Attica under Archidamus. Fighting occurred at Platea, Potidea, Methone, and Rhion, with Brasidas defending Methone and Phormio defeating the Lacedaemonian fleet. The unit also recounts the plague of Athens, the death and temporary political disgrace of Pericles, the surrender of Potidea, and the later naval victories of the Athenians.

l: the Peloponnesian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: The Peloponnesian war began between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians after disputes involving Megara and the wider rivalry between Athens and Sparta. The unit describes its causes, the opposing alliances, invasions of Attica and Peloponnesus, the siege of Potidea, and naval fighting at Rhion.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: The Athenians controlled a large alliance, possessed considerable wealth, and relied heavily on naval power. They invaded and plundered parts of Peloponnesus, defended Platea, besieged Potidea, expelled the inhabitants of Aegina, and suffered greatly from the plague.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: The Lacedaemonians supported the Megareans, declared war against the Athenians, and invaded Attica under Archidamus. They also gathered allies, sought Persian support, fought at sea against Phormio, and later withdrew after suffering naval defeats.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Athens brought the money held at Delos into the city and used its wealth, fleet, allies, and fortifications in the war. The city received refugees from the countryside during Lacedaemonian invasions, but overcrowding contributed to the plague.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Sparta acted with the Lacedaemonians in supporting Megara and opposing Athens. The text describes Sparta as poorer than Athens and inferior in naval forces.

l: Pericles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Pericles argued against rescinding the decree against Megara and persuaded the Athenians to resist the Lacedaemonians. He directed naval operations against Peloponnesus, was praised for his command, was later deprived of the magistracy and fined thirty talents, was recalled, and eventually died at Athens.

l: Alcibiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Alcibiades, who was under age and in the care of Pericles, advised him to consider how he might avoid giving an account of the money entrusted to him. His advice led Pericles to seek a great war as a way to escape the financial inquiry.

l: Megara, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Megara was subjected to an Athenian decree forbidding its people to trade with the Athenians by sea or land. The Megareans appealed to the Spartans, who demanded that Athens rescind the decree.

l: Athenian navy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: The Athenian navy included hundreds of ships and was presented by Pericles as a major advantage over the Lacedaemonians. Athenian fleets raided Peloponnesus, attacked coastal towns and castles, and won important engagements under Phormio.

l: Plataea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Plateaea was a free city allied with Athens when Theban forces and local traitors attempted to seize it. Its inhabitants defeated many of the invading Thebans, received Athenian assistance, and later resisted Archidamus when he besieged the city.

l: Archidamus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Archidamus was made general by the Lacedaemonians and led an invasion of Attica, where his army besieged castles and devastated the country. He later invaded Boeotia, sought to make Platea revolt, and besieged the city without taking it.

l: Attica, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Attica was invaded twice by the Lacedaemonians and their allies, who cut down trees, burned towns, and devastated much of the countryside. The Athenians largely remained within their walls during the second invasion.

l: Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Peloponnesus was repeatedly attacked by Athenian fleets under Pericles and other commanders. The Athenians raided its coasts, destroyed castles, burned towns, and plundered the country.

l: Brasidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Brasidas, a young Spartan of great strength and courage, entered Methone through the Athenian forces when the city was threatened. He helped preserve the city and gained high honor among the Spartans for his defense.

l: plague of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: The plague of Athens spread while the population was crowded inside the city during the Lacedaemonian invasion of Attica. It killed many people, weakened the Athenians, and contributed to their anger against Pericles.

l: Potidea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Potidea was the first city to make a defection from the Athenians and was besieged by an Athenian army. After its surrender, its inhabitants left with severely limited possessions and settled among the Chalcidicans in Thrace, while Athens sent a colony to occupy the city and surrounding country.

l: siege of Potidea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: The siege of Potidea lasted through repeated assaults and caused heavy Athenian losses from fighting and disease. The besiegers lost more than a thousand men before Potidea surrendered on terms requiring all inhabitants to leave with only limited clothing.

l: Phormio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: Phormio was made Athenian admiral and sailed with twenty ships to Naupactus, where he blocked the Lacedaemonian fleet. At Rhion he defeated a fleet of forty-seven ships, sank the admiral's vessel, captured twelve ships, and later fought the Lacedaemonians again until they withdrew toward Corinth.

l: Athenian victory at Rhion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: At Rhion, Phormio and twenty Athenian ships defeated the Lacedaemonian fleet of forty-seven ships. The Athenians sank the admiral's ship, captured twelve vessels with their crews, erected a trophy, and dedicated a ship to Neptune.

l: thirty years' truce, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. Vlf. /
s: The text states in its heading that a peace was concluded after the war had continued for ten years. It does not provide further details about the Thirty Years' Peace in this unit.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Sitalces of Thrace invaded Macedonia with a large army to support the Athenians, restore Amyntas, and oppose Perdiccas, but he later made peace with Perdiccas and withdrew. The Athenians sent a major expedition to Sicily under Lachetes, Chabrias, Eurymedon, and Sophocles, but returned after the Leontines made peace with the Syracusans. Lesbos revolted from Athens, and the Athenians besieged and captured Mitylene before sparing its inhabitants and dividing most of Lesbos among themselves. The Lacedaemonians captured Plataea and killed its defenders, while plague and famine continued to afflict Athens.

l: Sitalces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Sitalces, king of Thrace, greatly enlarged his dominions through valor and prudence and had an annual revenue of more than a thousand talents. He invaded Macedonia with more than 120,000 foot and 50,000 horse to assist the Athenians, oppose Perdiccas, and restore Amyntas, but later made peace with Perdiccas, confirmed it by marriage, and withdrew into Thrace.

l: Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Perdiccas, king of Macedonia, was opposed by Sitalces, who intended to restore Amyntas to his father's kingdom. He eventually made peace with Sitalces and sealed the agreement by marriage.

l: Amyntas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Amyntas, the son of Philip, was brought with the Thracians as the intended king of Macedonia. His restoration was one of the reasons for Sitalces's invasion.

l: Gorgias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Gorgias, an eloquent orator from Leontium, led the embassy requesting Athenian aid. His elaborate speech persuaded the Athenians to form a league with the Leontines.

l: Paches, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Paches, son of Epiderus, commanded the Athenian forces sent to Lesbos. After joining the earlier army at Mitylene, he tightened the siege and attacked the city by sea and land.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Athenians fought the Lacedaemonians and their allies, supported the Leontines in Sicily, besieged Mitylene, and divided most of Lesbos among themselves after the revolt. They also suffered severely from plague and famine, and their forces lost many men to disease.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Lacedaemonians attacked the Pyreum, invaded Attica under Archidamus, supported Mitylene, and besieged Plataea. They captured Plataea, executed its defenders, destroyed the city, and sent colonists to Trachinia, which they renamed Heraclea.

l: Thracians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Thracians followed Sitalces into Macedonia with a very large army. They brought Amyntas with them, captured a castle, received the surrender of several cities, plundered Macedonia, and then moved toward the Greek cities of Chalcidica.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Macedonians were terrified by the size of the Thracian army and did not oppose it in open battle. They gathered their goods and crops into their garrisons and forts, while some cities later surrendered.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Greeks living between Macedonia and Thermopylae, including Thessalians, Achaeans, and Magnesians, formed a confederacy and raised an army against the Thracians. Greek forces also included the cities and peoples involved in the wars in Sicily, Lesbos, and Plataea.

l: Chalcidicans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Chalcidicans joined the other Greeks in raising an army against Sitalces. They were also the people of Chalcidica whom the Athenians intended to attack with Sitalces's assistance.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Syracusans made war on Leontium and later received the Leontines into Syracuse. They made the Leontines free of Syracuse and turned Leontium into a Syracusan fort or garrison.

l: Leontines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Leontines appealed to Athens for aid against the Syracusans, and Gorgias persuaded the Athenians to form a league with them. During the Athenian campaign, they made peace with Syracuse, after which the Athenian fleet returned home.

l: Corcyreans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Corcyreans had earlier received Athenian support against the Corinthians because Corcyra offered a convenient passage toward Sicily. Later, Corcyrean prisoners promised to deliver Corcyra to the Corinthians in exchange for their release, but the Athenians assisted the Corcyreans, restored their freedom, and returned them to the city.

l: Lesbians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The inhabitants of Lesbos revolted from the Athenians after the inhabitants of its cities were removed and brought into Mitylene. They allied with the Lacedaemonians and promised to provide them with many ships.

l: Mityleneans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Mityleneans were defeated in a sea-fight by the Athenians and then besieged. After suffering from famine, warfare, and sedition, they surrendered the city.

l: Plateans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Plateans endured a long siege, shortages of provisions, and the loss of many citizens. Some escaped to Athens by breaking through the besiegers' defenses, while those remaining eventually surrendered and were executed by the Lacedaemonians.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Athens sent fleets and armies to Sicily and Lesbos and intervened in the affairs of Corcyra. It was also afflicted by plague and famine, while its people attributed the disease partly to divine displeasure and purified Delos.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Sicily was sought by the Athenians because of its fertile soil and wealth. The Athenians campaigned there against the Syracusans and their allies, but their expedition ended after the Leontines made peace with Syracuse.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Macedonia was invaded and plundered by Sitalces and the Thracians. Amyntas was brought forward as its intended king, while Perdiccas defended his position by making peace with Sitalces.

l: Chalcidica, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Chalcidica was a target of the Athenians and Sitalces. Its Greek cities joined a broader confederacy because they feared an invasion by the powerful Thracians.

l: Attica, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Attica was invaded by the Lacedaemonians and their allies under Archidamus. They destroyed the standing corn and ravaged the countryside while the Athenians, weakened by plague and famine, did not oppose them.

l: Leontium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
