s: Leontium, a colony founded by Chalcidicans and originally by Athenians, was threatened by Syracuse and appealed to Athens for aid. After the Leontines made peace with the Syracusans, Leontium became a Syracusan fort or garrison.

l: Lesbos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Lesbos revolted from Athens and allied with the Lacedaemonians. After Mitylene surrendered, the Athenians demolished its walls and divided the rest of the island among themselves, except for the lands belonging to Methymna.

l: Mitylene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Mitylene was besieged by the Athenians after its people revolted from Athens. When famine and internal disorder forced its surrender, the Athenians debated severe punishment but ultimately spared the inhabitants, while demolishing the city's walls.

l: Plataea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: Plataea was surrounded by Lacedaemonian walls, forts, and guards after a prolonged siege. The city surrendered when its defenders were distressed by hunger and losses, and the Lacedaemonians destroyed it after executing its remaining defenders.

l: Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Lacedaemonians and their confederates repeatedly came out of Peloponnesus to invade Attica. Peloponnesian settlers also joined the Lacedaemonian colony sent to Trachinia.

l: the Peloponnesian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The war involved repeated Lacedaemonian invasions of Attica, Athenian campaigns in Sicily and Lesbos, the siege and destruction of Plataea, and severe plague and famine at Athens.

l: Athenian expedition to Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Athenians sent fleets under Lachetes, Chabrias, Eurymedon, and Sophocles to support Leontium and pursue their larger designs in Sicily. They raided the Lipari islands, fought near the Myleans, captured a Locrian castle, and returned home after the Leontines made peace with Syracuse.

l: Lesbian revolt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The revolt began when the inhabitants of Lesbos opposed Athenian measures that removed the inhabitants of its cities to Mitylene. The rebels sought Lacedaemonian support, but the Athenians sent forces under Paches, besieged Mitylene, and imposed their settlement after its surrender.

l: siege of Plataea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The Lacedaemonians maintained a long siege of Plataea and built walls, forts, and guards around the city. Some Plateans escaped to Athens, but the remainder surrendered and were executed, and Plataea was destroyed.

l: plague at Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Diotinus executing the place of chief magistrate at Athens, the
s: The plague at Athens was accompanied by famine and was attributed in the account to wet weather, stagnant and polluted water, spoiled food, and the absence of the usual Etesian winds. Many Athenians suffered burning illnesses, and the city lost large numbers of soldiers, cavalry, servants, and others.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: The unit concerns the continuing war between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians, including Demosthenes’s campaigns in western Greece and the fortification and siege of Pylos. The Spartans and their allies failed to take Pylos, and the Athenians captured the Spartan and allied soldiers trapped on the Sphacterian island. Nicias later led Athenian operations against Melos, Boeotia, Corinth, Cythera, and the Peloponnesian coast, while Brasidas expanded Lacedaemonian influence in Megara, Thrace, and Amphipolis. The Boeotians defeated the Athenians at the Battle of Delium and subsequently captured Delium.

l: Demosthenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Demosthenes commanded Athenian forces in Acarnania, where he defeated Amb্রacian troops and destroyed much of the strength of Ambracia, but the Acarnanians refused to follow him in an assault on the city. He later fortified Pylos and defended it against the Lacedaemonians, and he also participated with Hippocrates in an unsuccessful attempt to secure Megara through treachery.

l: Brasidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Brasidas distinguished himself during the fighting at Pylos by forcing his ship ashore and bravely engaging the Athenians, though he was severely wounded and lost his shield. He later relieved Megara, brought several Thracian communities to the Lacedaemonian side, and captured Amphipolis, Torone, and other neighboring places.

l: Nicias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Nicias commanded Athenian naval expeditions against Melos, Boeotia, Corinth, Cythera, and the Peloponnesian coast. He won engagements against the Corinthians, captured Cremmyon, fortified Methone, took Cythera, and captured and demolished Thyrea.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: The Athenians conducted numerous naval and land operations against the Lacedaemonians and their allies. They successfully defended Pylos, captured the soldiers on the Sphacterian island, took Nicea at Megara, and suffered a major defeat against the Boeotians at Delium.

l: Spartans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: The Spartans sent forces by land and sea to attack Pylos and placed chosen soldiers on the Sphacterian island. After the island was blockaded and provisions were stopped, 120 Spartans surrendered with their allies and were taken to Athens.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: The Lacedaemonians attempted to recover Pylos, sent ambassadors to Athens to seek peace or an exchange of prisoners, and eventually lost the soldiers trapped on the Sphacterian island. They later sent Brasidas reinforcements, including 1,000 Helots, and supported his operations in Megara, Thrace, and Amphipolis.

l: Boeotians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: The Boeotians gathered a large army under Pantoedas and defeated the Athenians at Delium. They pursued the Athenians, killed many of them, captured Delium after further fighting, and used the spoils to build and adorn public works and establish games.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Athens received the Lacedaemonian and allied prisoners captured on the Sphacterian island and decreed that they would be preserved if the Lacedaemonians ended the war, but killed if the war continued. Athens also sent forces under Nicias against several Lacedaemonian allies and supplied workmen for the fortification of Nicea.

l: Naupactus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Naupactus was inhabited by the Messenians and was threatened by the Aetolians and Lacedaemonians. Demosthenes sent 1,000 men from Acarnania to strengthen its garrison.

l: Pylos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Pylos was naturally fortified, and Demosthenes surrounded it with a wall in twenty days. The Athenians defended it against a large Lacedaemonian land and sea force, and its possession enabled them to threaten Laconia and block supplies to the Sphacterian island.

l: Sphacteria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Sphacteria was an island near the entrance of the harbor at Pylos. The Lacedaemonians placed chosen soldiers there, but the Athenian fleet blockaded the island and forced its defenders to surrender.

l: Laconia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Laconia was exposed to Athenian attack after the Athenians established themselves at Pylos and later placed Messenians in its garrison. Athenian forces also raided its coastal areas and attacked places near its borders.

l: Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Peloponnesus became a major theater of the war after the Athenians fortified Pylos. Athenian forces later raided its coasts and captured places including Thyrea.

l: Boeotia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Boeotia was invaded by Athenian forces after malcontents promised to deliver its cities to them. The invasion failed politically, and the Boeotians defeated the Athenians at Delium.

l: Megara, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Megara was divided by conflict between factions favoring the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians. Athenian troops entered through a conspiracy, besieged the Lacedaemonians in Nicea, and then lost their position when Brasidas arrived and restored Megara to Lacedaemonian obedience.

l: Amphipolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Amphipolis had experienced repeated changes of population and control before Brasidas attacked it. Its inhabitants surrendered to Brasidas on terms allowing those who wished to leave to take their effects, after which Brasidas used it as a base for further operations.

l: Delium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Delium was occupied and fortified by Hippocrates and the Athenians near Oropus and the borders of Boeotia. The Boeotians later assaulted it, killed much of its garrison, captured 200 defenders, and forced the remaining Athenians to escape.

l: Pylos siege, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: The Lacedaemonians besieged Pylos with land forces and a fleet of forty-five ships, attacking the walls repeatedly while trying to block the harbor. The Athenians resisted, and the siege ended with the Lacedaemonians losing control of the Sphacterian island and surrendering its defenders.

l: Battle of Delium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: The Battle of Delium was fought between the Athenians and the Boeotians after the Athenians fortified Delium. The Boeotians won after their Theban forces routed the Athenian troops opposing them, and the Athenians fled toward Oropus, Delium, and their ships.

l: capture of the Sphacterian prisoners, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: The Athenians captured 120 Spartans and 180 of their confederates after the soldiers on the Sphacterian island were starved and forced to submit. Cleon brought the prisoners bound to Athens, where their fate was made conditional on whether the Lacedaemonians ended the war.

l: the Peloponnesian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: The Peloponnesian War in this unit involved Athenian and Lacedaemonian operations across western Greece, Peloponnesus, Boeotia, Megara, and Thrace. Major developments included the fortification of Pylos, the capture of the Sphacterian prisoners, Brasidas’s expansion around Amphipolis, and the Boeotian victory at Delium.

l: fortification at Pylos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: Demosthenes built a wall around Pylos in twenty days because the site was naturally strong and well supplied. The fortification survived repeated Lacedaemonian assaults and became the base from which the Athenians controlled the sea and threatened Laconia.

l: Sphacterian island, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Stratocies being archon of Athens, the consular dignity was con-
s: The Sphacterian island lay near the harbor of Pylos and was considered useful for securing the harbor and supporting the siege. Lacedaemonian and allied soldiers stationed there were cut off from supplies by the Athenian fleet and eventually surrendered.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, In Asia, Xerxes the Persian king died, after lie had reigned one
s: The unit concerns the conflict between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians during the Peloponnesian War, especially the struggle over Scione and other cities in Thrace. Nicias and Nicostratus besiege Scione, while Cleon later campaigns against Torone and advances toward Amphipolis. At the battle near Amphipolis, both Cleon and Brasidas are killed, and the Lacedaemonians win. The Athenians and Lacedaemonians then make peace, ending the ten-year war.

l: Brasidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, In Asia, Xerxes the Persian king died, after lie had reigned one
s: Brasidas was the Lacedaemonian general in Thrace who protected Scione and Menda and placed strong garrisons in them. He later fought Cleon near Amphipolis, where he was killed in the battle.

l: Nicias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, In Asia, Xerxes the Persian king died, after lie had reigned one
s: Nicias was sent with Nicostratus and fifty ships against Scione. He first helped take Menda and then besieged Scione by surrounding it with a wall and making continual assaults.

l: Cleon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, In Asia, Xerxes the Persian king died, after lie had reigned one
s: Cleon led a large Athenian force to the coasts of Thrace, took Torone, and marched toward Scione and Amphipolis. He fought Brasidas near Amphipolis and was killed in the battle.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, In Asia, Xerxes the Persian king died, after lie had reigned one
s: The Athenians fought to recover Scione and other cities that had defected to the Lacedaemonians. They besieged Scione, expelled the Delians from their island, and later agreed to peace with the Lacedaemonians after the deaths of Cleon and Brasidas.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, In Asia, Xerxes the Persian king died, after lie had reigned one
s: The Lacedaemonians received Scione's defection and placed it under Brasidas's protection. They defeated the Athenians near Amphipolis and then made a peace agreement requiring the release of prisoners and the restoration of cities taken during the war.
